subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. I wonder whether the Prime Minister has had an opportunity to conduct the necessary consultations and can now say whether the proposed meeting of the continuing committee of the Prime Minister and the provincial premiers on the constitution will be held before Christmas as planned.
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wrote to all the premiers of the provinces a few days ago, following my earlier letter of two weeks ago, suggesting that the general assessment of the situation at that time was that most provinces might be agreeable to a date early in December, around December 8 or 9 if my memory is correct. However, I did indicate in these letters that I had written a different kind of letter to the premier of Quebec and the premier of Alberta, in view of the recent situation which has developed in those countries-

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext: He has been talking to the hon. member for Calgary South.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext: For some of you country boys I think this would be welcome.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext: Check Hansard on that one.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not correct Hansard the same as those hon. members.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Order, please. I wonder
whether the Prime Minister is now addressing the chair.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO MEETING OF CONTINUING COMMITTEE
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker-indicating that in view of the particular situation in those two provinces we might give leeway to the two premiers in suggesting an alternative date, but that it was still our hope to have the meeting on the dates suggested in December. We are awaiting replies, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to address a question to the Minister without Portfolio who acts in the place of the Minister of Transport, who has responsibility for housing and according to the schedule is supposed to be here today.
I should like to ask the Acting Minister of Transport whether he can assure the house that the $170 million the Minister of Transport announced would be made available to private developers and builders for building family units will not in any way reduce the amount of money to be made available this year for public housing.
October 8, 1968

Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will be very glad to look into that question and report to the hon. member.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I address a supplementary question to the Prime Minister, who I understand is responsible as to which ministers should or should not be here. May I ask him whether he and his government can assure the house and the country that the $170 million now being made available for private building purposes does not in any way reduce the amount of money that is also available for public housing, as originally intended.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what is the objection to having the Acting Minister of Transport answer this question when he has the information?

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext:
He
has not got the information.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: Nor has the Prime Minister. I am asking the Prime Minister whether he and the government can give us this assurance, and as Prime Minister of this country he ought to be in a position to do so.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: If the hon. member is more interested in having information than in scoring debating points, then surely he should have no objection to being given the correct information within 24 hours.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I do not care whether it is the Prime Minister or anyone else.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: He has no right to impute motives to any member of this house, and I resent his suggestion.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: On that point of order, Mr. Speaker, I say I am entirely in order in asking the Prime Minister for the assurance that this amount will not be reduced.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOCATION OF FUNDS BETWEEN PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member is quite right. It is a basic rule of debate that no hon. member may impute motives.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLACEMENT FOR WINTER WORKS PROGRAM

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLACEMENT FOR WINTER WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the right honourable Prime Minister.

When does he intend to introduce his just society policy to replace the winter works policy, in view of the fact that municipalities are now in a very difficult situation?
Can the house expect an early statement from the right hon. Prime Minister in this connection?

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLACEMENT FOR WINTER WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the policy in this regard was launched before cancelling the winter works program; this the member should know.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLACEMENT FOR WINTER WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of
order.
We are precisely asking the Prime Minister to inform the house about the work done so far by the government, because the Canadian people are not aware of it.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO REPLACEMENT FOR WINTER WORKS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I
announced the end of winter works, I explained that they had been replaced by programs entailing much higher and much more useful expenditures as far as the economic expansion of the country is concerned.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REQUEST FOR REPORT RESPECTING CONSIDERATION OF SHARED PROGRAMS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REQUEST FOR REPORT RESPECTING CONSIDERATION OF SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the Prime Minister indicated that the government was endeavouring to hold meetings of federal and provincial ministers of finance or treasury officials with a view to discussing open ended joint programs. Will the Prime Minister kindly clarify the situation that has developed? Will those meetings he referred to be part of the general dominion-provincial meetings with regard to dominion-provincial financial arrangements, or will they be separate meetings?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REQUEST FOR REPORT RESPECTING CONSIDERATION OF SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: They would be part of the meetings of the ministers of finance of the federal government and the provinces. There may also have to be separate meetings of health and welfare ministers.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REQUEST FOR REPORT RESPECTING CONSIDERATION OF SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In those supplementary meetings will medicare and its position in the open ended programs listed by the government be part of the discussion?
October 8, 1968

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS REQUEST FOR REPORT RESPECTING CONSIDERATION OF SHARED PROGRAMS
speechtext: We have indicated, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces are free to put any item they wish on the agenda. If they want to put medicare on, that would certainly be acceptable.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH NEWSPAPER OFFICIALS ON REDUCTION IN SERVICE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH NEWSPAPER OFFICIALS ON REDUCTION IN SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Postmaster General. Can the Postmaster General report to this house how the discussions with the circulation managers of daily newspapers are proceeding? I ask this question in view of the minister's announcement in this house last week end that discussions would be taking place in this regard early this week, with a view to altering the announced Saturday cutoff in mail delivery.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH NEWSPAPER OFFICIALS ON REDUCTION IN SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since yesterday morning field directors and officers of the post office have been fanning out across the country to discuss with publishers and circulation managers of newspapers the problems occasioned by the ending of postal deliveries on Saturday. I may say that the reaction has been extremely warm.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH NEWSPAPER OFFICIALS ON REDUCTION IN SERVICE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH NEWSPAPER OFFICIALS ON REDUCTION IN SERVICE
speechtext: The editors and circulation managers of newspapers have appreciated the delicatesse of the officers of the department as well as their anxiety to find ways of easing whatever problems may arise. We are pursuing this program, and when the reports come in from the field I anticipate holding a general meeting with the senior executives of the association itself.

subtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH NEWSPAPER OFFICIALS ON REDUCTION IN SERVICE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Since the minister has indicated that he is seeking reports on the matter, is he prepared to accept reports from hon. members of this house on behalf of their constituents? I have several hundred right now on my desk.

Inquiries of the Ministry and Rural Development to the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO POSSIBLE MERGER AND APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO POSSIBLE MERGER AND APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Winnipeg South, in connection with the task force on Air Canada. Could he advise the house how that task force is proceeding and whether any evidence has been placed before him or those associated with him, or whether representations have been made, that Air Canada should merge with Canadian Pacific Airlines, a suggestion which received support from the hon. gentleman in June?

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO POSSIBLE MERGER AND APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: I have been asked by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Transport to look into the future planning of Air Canada. One of many alternatives which exist is a possible merger, but no active consideration is being given at the present time to a merger of Air Canada and Canadian Pacific.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO POSSIBLE MERGER AND APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: I thank the minister for that answer, and would ask him whether his views have changed since June when he said Air Canada and Canadian Pacific should join together and the stock be made available for private purchase.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO POSSIBLE MERGER AND APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: I thought the minister was about to answer the question addressed to him by my right hon. friend. Has the minister been able as yet to recommend to his colleagues the name of a new president for Air Canada?

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO POSSIBLE MERGER AND APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext:
I think I should say first of all that the board of directors of Air Canada and the government are well pleased with the interim management which is being given to Air Canada by the acting president. I should

October 8, 1968
Inquiries of the Ministry say further that the board of directors are considering changes in the management structure of the company and that these changes are being discussed with the government.

subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO POSSIBLE MERGER AND APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman intended to answer my question but did not get the opportunity. I would not wish to deny him-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: INQUIRIES AS TO POSSIBLE MERGER AND APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: Order. It might be helpful if I suggested that the question was not entirely in order. The right hon. gentleman is asking whether the minister has changed his views. That in itself, I suggest, is not a proper question.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: CHURCHILL-INQUIRY INTO EXTENSION OF SEASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the other day the Minister of Transport said he would be looking into the report on the possibility of the extension of the shipping season at Churchill, may I ask the Acting Minister of Transport whether that report will be made public.
Inquiries of the Ministry

subtopic: CHURCHILL-INQUIRY INTO EXTENSION OF SEASON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been continuous examination of the extension of the Churchill shipping season, and there have been investigations, particularly into new ice breaking techniques which would enable the port seasons to be extended.

subtopic: CHURCHILL-INQUIRY INTO EXTENSION OF SEASON
speechtext: Will these reports be made public or will they be secret documents for the department's own use?

subtopic: CHURCHILL-INQUIRY INTO EXTENSION OF SEASON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Transport, and in view of the fact that we were unable to obtain a reply from the acting minister, will the right hon. Prime Minister undertake to consult with someone in the department to determine whether there is a report on a possible extension of the Churchill shipping season, and whether this report will be made public?

subtopic: CHURCHILL-INQUIRY INTO EXTENSION OF SEASON
speechtext: Surely the acting minister attempted to reply earlier, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: CHURCHILL-INQUIRY INTO EXTENSION OF SEASON
speechtext: He attempted; that's right.

subtopic: CHURCHILL-INQUIRY INTO EXTENSION OF SEASON
speechtext: We all make attempts. You sometimes attempt to ask questions.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CHURCHILL-INQUIRY INTO EXTENSION OF SEASON

Such a tribute to our post office employees, however, would be meaningless if it were not accompanied by a resolve to improve their working conditions, enhance employee job satisfaction and open up opportunities for advancement, self-improvement and fuller personal development. These are the elements that an employee looks for in a just society and by which he will judge that society.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
The Post Office Department has accomplished a great deal in this area, credit for which must go to my immediate predecessor, the hon. member for Longueuil. Most of the 48,000 public servants in the Post Office Department are now covered by collective bargaining. Greater security of employment increases confidence, invites participation and inspires loyalty and pride. Agreements recently concluded with the union will provide better working conditions of employment for the operating staff, approximately 28,000 employees. Contrary to the impression of some who were inconvenienced by the long postal strike, it is true to say, and I am glad to confirm, that the leaders of the postal union demonstrated during this period their sense of responsibility and respect for the law. That law in a just society must always give to all groups the power to fight for and to defend their rights. A just society, Mr. Chairman, depends on a thriving economy, for only an efficient, expanding economy can afford the costs of rectifying injustices, improving distributions of wealth and incomes and hope to reduce the burden of poverty.
The institutions of such an economy and such a society must be efficient and thriving.

The post office is such an institution. Our function is communication, the transmission at low cost of items of business and personal information from one place to another. In this function we complement, we duplicate, but to an increasing extent are being superseded by other systems of communication, telephone, teletype machines, telegraph, television, radio and the cloud that appears no bigger than a hand, satellites.
Nearly all of the important innovations in communications are taking place outside the post office and indeed outside the existing governmental structure. What effect, for example, will such developments as television-telephones, telephones linked to computers for information retrival or even the payment of household bills, newspaper delivery direct to homes via television or teletype, what effect will these technical possibilities and soon to be economically feasible changes have on the traditional function of the post office, the transmission of information? These developments are taking place outside the post office and outside of the government; rather, I should say they were taking place outside of the post office and outside of the government. For now we are to have a department of communications of which the post office will be an integral part. The post office will have, therefore, at its disposal in the future the best scientists in the research branch of the department of communications to enable it to meet the challenge of change. This has already been agreed upon by the officers of the post office and officers-designate of the new department.
The creation of the new department is clear evidence of the government's belief that for a just society we must have not only a thriving economy but modern institutions, institutions aware of today's realities and alive to tomorrow's possibilities. Clearly, the post office was viewed by the Prime Minister, when he proposed this reorganization, as a problem of function, of communications in a rapidly changing industry, not as the perennial problem of an institution in political, financial or administrative difficulties.
It is a new view, a new idea that must be accepted by all of us. The difficulty will lie, I suspect, not so much in accepting these new ideas, if I may paraphrase Lord Keynes, but in escaping from the old ones. The Post Office Department is faced with a great many problems. One of the most serious is the mounting cost of its own operations departmental forecasts indicate that on the basis of present fees and postage rates the post office accounts
October 8, 1968

will show a deficit of $99.5 million in the current fiscal year. At the same time there is a pressing need to improve services, to modernize and extend the facilities and improve working conditions, all of which will require increased expenditures.
It is evident, therefore, that action must be taken to restore a reasonable cost-revenue relationship, and to provide the funds necessary to ensure that our traditional standard of service will be maintained. Hon. members of the committee are aware that I have already taken action to adjust the rates charged for those classes of mail which, under the Post Office Act, the Postmaster General may regulate. It is expected that these rates will result in revenues equal to the costs of handling the classes of mail concerned.
Some studies have begun, and others are pending, which will search out ways and means of reducing costs, improving administration and productivity, and of achieving the most effective staff relations. Broadly speaking, these actions comprise what the Postmaster General can do on his own authority. As examples I may cite the closing of the postal savings bank, the move to a five day week, and the decision to make those who use our money order system pay the reasonable costs of operating that system. Many other changes leading to greater efficiency are also being considered. The public, Mr. Chairman, will not forgive us if we seek to balance our budget solely by rate increases. Our responsibility is to examine all procedures, all traditional methods, to gauge their worthiness and present efficacy. Cutting out the fat, the outmoded, is painful but it is also necessary.
This brings me to the bill to be considered by this house. Its major items have to do with adjustments to the rates fixed by statute with respect to letters, newspapers and periodicals, that is, first and second class mail. The present rates for local and out of town letters took effect on April 1, 1954. In the 14 years since that date, costs of all kinds have increased sharply, including the cost of operating the postal service. Our cost analyses show that the cost of handling letter mail now exceeds the revenue derived from it. Moreover, it has been found that the cost of handling letters for local delivery, commonly known as drop letters, has increased at an accelerated rate, so that the average cost of handling a letter mailed for delivery in the same locality is not noticeably less than that of a letter delivered through a post office other than the one at which it was mailed. We are no longer justified, therefore, in
Post Office Act
maintaining a lower rate of postage for local letters. Canada is virtually the only postal administration in the world providing unlimited local delivery of letters at a lower rate of postage, and it is clear that we cannot continue to do so in the light of mounting postal deficits.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The proposed rates applicable to letters mailed in Canada for delivery anywhere in Canada are six cents for the first ounce or fraction and four cents for each additional ounce or fraction. I might add that we have in mind in connection with these increases a quid pro quo whereby all letter mail posted in Canada for delivery in Canada will be carried by air where this will expedite delivery. The committee is aware that Canada pioneered this "all-up" service for letters up to one ounce in weight in 1948, an innovation by the Liberal government of the time. The removal of the present weight limit of eight ounces, which was established in 1954, will no doubt be welcomed by the business world.
The proposed changes respecting newspapers and periodicals are intended to accomplish two main objectives: first, to take a long step toward assuring that this class of mail pays its fair share of the operation by substantially increasing the rates of postage applicable to it; second, to amend and clarify the terms and conditions under which the statutory second class rates apply. These changes will provide a substantial amount of additional revenue and a more logical basis for determining entitlement to second class privileges.
The remaining changes in the Post Office Act are intended to clarify the authority and responsibility of the Postmaster General with respect to some aspects of departmental administration, and to facilitate the adjustment of transportation arrangements so that we can keep up with changing conditions.
In addition, two amendments are sought in connection with the winding up of the Post Office Savings Bank. As the committee is aware from the announcement recently made, the government has decided to discontinue this service because of the steady decline in the number of depositors, the amounts deposited and the total balance on deposit. It has been evident for some time that there is little need and almost no demand for this facility. It is no part of a just society to pay 1\ per cent interest to depositors when they can more than double their income by investing in Canada savings bonds.

I believe it is unnecessary for me to say more by way of introduction. I would, however, assure the committee that I will do my utmost to answer fully and frankly the questions of the opposition during the clause by clause consideration of the bill. The department is quite prepared to lay before this house the most detailed information on its operations, with the hope of receiving the constructive criticisms and suggestions of all members interested in a postal service that will provide a standard of excellence that will be the pride of all Canadians.
This is the challenge before this committee, Mr. Chairman. I would remind hon. members that no substantial legislation has been passed affecting first class rates since 1954. No substantial legislation has been passed affecting second class rates since 1951. The question before us is: Are we to bring the post office into the modern era as a living, changing force, or are we to turn back the clock to 1951 and 1954 and condemn the department to exist in the strait-jacket of outmoded rates, regulations and procedures? That is the choice before us.
Under our parliamentary system, the government proposes but this house disposes. I would not have it otherwise. With every confidence in the wisdom and judgment of all members of the house, I move the adoption of this resolution.

There is something even more important than that that we ought to consider. I say to the minister, the matter is not nearly as simple as he made it appear when he spoke about 80 per cent of business being done on five days of the week. I say that this change will impose a serious problem on many established businesses at the very same time that the increased rate will present those businesses with other difficult problems. The minister has made no case for Saturday closing. His brief explanation of a few weeks ago was as inadequate as it was unwelcome. I have read many reports of experts who have examined one phase or another of our postal operation, reports of experts such as those with the Glassco commission, but I have yet to read any report which recommended as a solution to any problem the closing of post offices on Saturday. Indeed, a study of commercial operations in this country will indicate that Saturday is one of the busiest days of the week. There has been a change in recent years in the week end business pattern. There are many Canadians who derive no great satisfaction from the institutions of government. There are many Canadians in humble circumstances who receive from their government very little which means more to them than the rapid and efficient delivery of

mail whether it be in connection with business, whether it be in the nature of communications from their loved ones, or what have you. In our mobile society the curtailment of rapid communication by letter is something I find hard to accept. I find it even harder to accept the suggestion that in some way we advance the just society by so doing.
I was impressed the other day by an indication of lack of careful thought which has gone into this proposal. In answer to a question a brittle reply was given that the rural carriers would, of course, have their returns diminished to five-sixths of what they were. Mathematically, this sounds good. But what in the name of goodness will happen to the men whose already far too small earnings will be so diminished? Will they find an alternative job to make up for the decline in their incomes, and will they find one just for the now free Saturday? To make this kind of brittle, callous calculation indicates there is probably a good deal less compassion in the just society than we had hoped for.
I say: Let the mail go through. If a case can be made for increased charges there is no one so unreasonable as to suggest they must be opposed. But we are now faced with a situation in which the service will be diminished and the cost increased. Surely the post office is not in so bad a situation that both these things must be visited upon the people. I suggest to the minister that he take a little more care and go into this question a little more thoroughly, that the public be told more about what is to be done to their ancient institution, the post office. I should like the house and the committee to be told a little more about these things.
In my opinion-and my hon. friend from Oxford demonstrated today that it is his view also-this is a most unpopular move. In my opinion the people of Canada do not want their postal service curtailed as the minister has suggested. Canadians are concerned and many more are uncertain. Therefore I would strongly suggest that this proposed measure be referred to a committee of the house, either a standing or special committee, where witnesses may be heard, where people in the newspaper field can put forward their case plainly instead of expressing their heat to departmental field officers, where spokesmen for other businesses which are geared to the mail system as it now exists may explain their attitude, where the whole matter may be discussed and fully considered and where many of the matters not discussed by the minister today may be carefully canvassed.

This is a serious step, Mr. Chairman. It is one which involves the diminution of service, one which should not be made lightly after a casual announcement by a minister, however able he may be. I should like to be given more information on the publications issue which was referred to by the O'Leary commission and, in my opinion, never adequately dealt with. I should like to hear of any difficulties likely to be encountered in connection with the transmitting of bills of lading in relation to freight shipments. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was correct the other day when he said the Post Office Act should be amended so that parliament would have more control over postal rates than it has at present. When I worked in the office of the Postmaster General, I realized that the Canadian postal service is a very extensive operation. I met in this department employees who were always ready and willing to serve their country and to co-operate with the minister and senior officials.
As in any well-organized undertaking, the heads of this department are thoroughly informed about the operating costs and they are trying to hold the balance even between postal revenues and working expenses.
That is why on September 28, 1967, the hon. minister introduced in this house a bill designed to bring in annual revenues of more than $40 million. It is that same resolution that the opposition thought fit to turn down on November 28, 1967, thereby contributing to the increase of the deficit of the fiscal year ending on March 31, 1968.
For long years the department managed to balance its postal revenue and operating costs. The Canadian population was not increasing very rapidly. The volume of mail remained constant. Transportation and labour costs did not vary much. Because of these factors, it was possible to ensure well-balanced postal operations.

October 8. 1968
Post Office Act
Consequently, the last increase in postal rates-as pointed out by the hon. minister a while ago-goes back 14 years, to the time when the department provided, at no increase in costs, air transport within Canada for letters weighing less than eight ounces.
But things have changed since. Today, changes occur more rapidly than ever.
According to the last figures of the department, postal revenue amounted to $337 million compared to expenditures of $404,300,000 for operating costs. This means, as indicated in the report, a deficit of $67,200,000, which the parliament will have to make good.
Canadian postal expenses will not go down. As I said, times have changed.
Each time the Canadian population increases by one, the Post Office Department must handle 240 more pieces of mail per year.
Mr. Chairman, at the present time the mail volume, still according to the report of the department, amounts to almost 5 billion pieces. And, according to the statistics, the Canadian mail volume increases by 5 per cent every year. This means that in 14 years from now, the mail volume handled by the Post Office Department will be twice what it now is; and that 10 billion pieces will be handled annually. One may rightly say that the figure is impressive.
In his resolution, the minister proposes to increase from 50 to 60 the rate on first class letters. Let us not forget, in this regard, that the 5 cents rate has applied for over 14 years. Yet, the cost of transport and other costs have increased since.
Now, if we expect Canadian posts to pay their own way, mail rates must be increased.
Some 15 years ago, Canadians could get a cup of coffee for 5 cents, a bottle of Coke for 5 cents, a cigar for 5 cents. Today, these items have doubled in price, while we still pay in 1968, 5 cents to mail a letter out of town and 4 cents for local delivery.
The former Postmaster general who is now Minister of National Revenue, has carefully studied postal problems. During his term of office, more efficient methods of dealing with the mail have been adopted. I should like, Mr. Chairman, to mention some methods of delivering the mail that have been put into practice in a pilot area, the Gaspe peninsula.
The peninsula was a testing ground for a new method, which has since been extended to the whole of Canada: rural routes have been spread out from large centres.
TMr. Cyr.]
Several small revenue post offices have been closed down; thus better service was extended to users directly to their home, thanks to the setting up of rural routes.
According to the Canada Post Office's last annual report, 221 post offices were closed down between March 31, 1967 and March 31, 1968. Out of those 221 post offices, 63 were in the Gaspe and Bonaventure counties and 17 others will close down in a few months. This will bring the number to 80, and they are exclusively in the two constituencies I just mentioned. People who were using those post offices are getting their mail through rural routes' service.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, rural routes' service is much better than the letter carrier service in large cities. People using it can buy stamps from the rural letter carrier. The latter looks after registration of letters, parcel insurance, sale of money orders and collection of C.O.D. amounts. He is a sort of travelling post office with a fixed time-table, while the city letter carrier only delivers mail. The payment of contractors who deliver the mails on rural routes has been discussed for several years, and by your leave, Mr. Chairman, I will come back to that later on.
Another change made in the delivery service by the department, from 1966 to 1967, has been the establishment of serving centres designed to expedite transportation of mail on short distances and make it more efficient. These centres are located in well-defined geographical areas and the mail is quickly dispatched to these offices during the quiet hours of the night to be delivered afterwards by suboffices to neighbouring communities. In that way, and particularly in the Gaspe peninsula, the mail from Montreal and Quebec city is received several hours earlier than under the old transportation system. In many cases, the service enjoyed by expanding localities was poor because they were at the end of the railway line or the highway service. All that is changed now. It began in the pilot area of the Gaspe peninsula under the tenure of the 46th Postmaster General, the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Cote). Eighty of those centres are now operating, according to the annual report of the Post Office Department, and the creation of 120 other serving centres throughout the country is under study.
The merger of the small revenue post offices, the creation of new rural routes and serving centres are new services available to the Canadian people.
October 8, 1968

Mr. Chairman, the increases provided in the resolution now under consideration are not designed exclusively to pay for the new salaries of the post office employees. I gave other reasons why the 6c. rate now proposed by the minister is a bargain for the whole of Canada.
Canadians are willing to pay one cent more in postage for their letters because, in the last few years, the Post Office Department has been giving a much better service.
I would not like to see for any reason whatsoever the quality of the service go down after the passing of the bill which will be introduced in the house. It is necessary to establish the right balance between the revenue and the expenditures of the Post Office Department, but it must be remembered that the department must contribute to the progress of Canada and to the daily life of the people. It has discharged that obligation successfully until now and I am sure that Canadians from coast to coast are grateful to the postal employees. I wish to add in passing that Canada can be really proud of its postal service and, as stated by the minister earlier, it is the best in the world.
Mr. Chairman, while keeping to the resolution under consideration, I wish to refer to the report of the royal commission on working conditions in the Post Office Department.
At the time the late Rene Tremblay was holding the office of Postmaster General, there was a lot of unrest in the department. The employees were most anxious to have their own union and they asked urgently for the creation of a collective bargaining system. They were unhappy also about the method used to establish their pay level and job classification.
In July and August 1965 a strike was called in the main post offices in Canada. This was the first work stoppage by postal workers in forty years. While the strike was going on; Hon. Rene Tremblay was endeavouring behind the scenes to find some way of settling the differences between the demands of the employees and the offers of the government. The name of the former member for Matane, however, was never particularly mentioned in press releases and reports.
The Postmaster General wanted to get to the bottom of things. It is during his discussions with the leaders of the postal workers' unions that he agreed to establish a commission of inquiry on working conditions in the Post Office Department.
Post Office Act
Mr. Tremblay did not merely make that promise to the employees. He also convinced his colleagues in the cabinet concerning the need to establish such a commission as reported in order in council P.C. 1965-1590 which reads as follows:
The Committee of the Privy Council, on the recommendation of the Postmaster General, advise that Mr. Justice Andre Montpetit, Montreal, Quebec, be appointed a Commissioner-
Justice Montpetit presided during a 12 month period an investigation among the employees throughout Canada on their complaints about working conditions. When the report was tabled, it dealt with a great number of complaints stated under the form of a summary including 282 recommendations made by the commission.
Mr. Chairman, I must today, on this first opportunity which is given to me to speak in this house since the death of hon. Rene Tremblay, pay a tribute to this minister who left a most useful working paper for future Postmasters General and the authorities of the department.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AFFECTING RATES, ADMINISTRATION, SAVINGS BANK
speechtext:
Referring to the report of the royal commission, I shall mention particularly recommendation No. 58 which reads as follows:
That the responsible authorities conduct a thorough study of the consequences of the adoption of a policy aimed at curtailing postal service on week-ends.
Moreover, under recommendation No. 59, paragraph (c) we read:
That this study include amongst other things:
-the possibility of suspending postal operations between the midnight shift on Friday and the evening shift on Sunday at those locations where this is practical, i.e., where no serious delay in mail delivery would occur;
And under paragraph (d) we read:
The possibility in those offices where it would not be practical to curtail Saturday delivery and wicket service, of employing a minimum staff for the sale of money orders, etc., sorting, preparation and delivery of only first class mail matter along with C.O.D.'s and registered mail and the dispatching of mail of these classes.
Mr. Chairman, the resolution now before us purports to gather revenues to balance the budget of the department. As I said at the beginning, it is our duty, here in this house, to balance the budget of the Post Office Department. As I said right at the beginning, we have obligations towards Canada and its population, because the postal service belongs to the daily life of Canadians.

October 8, 1968
Post Office Act
On September 27, 1968 the Postmaster General declared, as reported in Hansard, page 496, that as from February 1, 1969, he intends to close the post offices on Saturdays. I quote:
It is, therefore, intended to close the post offices on Saturdays. Deliveries of mail will not be made on Saturdays. This will include letter carrier service, parcel post and rural route deliveries.
Mr. Chairman, I object to the closing of certain post offices in the morning on Saturdays as well as to stopping, on Saturdays, mail deliveries on rural routes.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the Post Office Department undertook in 1967 a program of amalgamation of all revenue post offices and establishment of rural routes for the delivery of mail to those who were no longer served by their post offices. The Postmaster General at that time told these people that the rural routes would provide them with better service. The program was very well received and the people served by the rural routes are very satisfied with the present service. Newspapers printed in Montreal or Quebec on Friday were distributed in Gaspe on Saturday afternoon or evening and, in some places, on Sunday morning. Thanks to the new delievery service established in 1967 and the distribution centres, the Friday editions of Montreal and Quebec newspapers reach the post offices in the ridings of Gaspe and Bonaventure during the night from Friday to Saturday, and they are delivered to the post offices and on the rural routes on Saturday morning. The people of Gaspe peninsula I represent are ready to accept a one cent increase on the postage rate of letters, as it is justified by the new postal services which have been placed at their disposal for more than one year.
According to the statement made on September 27 in the house by the minister to the effect that he was thinking of closing post offices on Saturdays, the people of Gaspe peninsula will receive their Friday papers on Monday only.
Mr. Chairman, this decision does not concern only the region of Gaspe but all the regions which are far from the large centres. Post office users in big cities like Montreal, Toronto, Ottawa, Quebec, Halifax, Vancouver, Winnipeg and others, can do without the post office service on Saturdays since the newspapers are printed in those cities and their citizens can buy them at any stand or have them delivered at home by newsboys.
[Mr. Cyr.l
Mr. Chairman, if the delivery of the mail is stopped on Saturdays, rural regions will regress by 50 years. The resolution is proposing measures affecting mail delivery and rate structure as applied to newspapers and periodicals. If we are to increase the statutory rate on Canadian newspapers-daily papers that is-I suggest to the hon. minister that the increase be sufficient to make sure that Canadians who now get their paper by mail on Saturdays will still get it.
As I said at the outset of my remarks, the Post Office Department has the responsibility to contribute to Canada's development and to the well-being of its people generally. I suggest it is not by discontinuing delivery of mail on Saturdays in rural areas that we shall reach that objective. The department is saving money by consolidating small postal substations and is still carrying on that program. It would be ill-timed to deprive the patrons of rural post offices, of their Saturday mail.
In his statement of September 27, the minister said: It is, therefore, intended to close the post offices on Saturdays." I take for granted that the decision is not final, since he used the word "intended".
Mr. Chairman, it would be proper more than ever to meditate on the Latin proverb taken from the book of the great Augustus, Festina lente-Make haste slowly.
The resolution now before us reads in part as follows:
-to provide for certain changes in connection with the administration of the act, more especially in relation to tenders and contracts-
The payment of services given by rural contractors has always been particularly emphasized in this house.
The basic rate is fixed according to norms taking into account the distance travelled, the number of boxes on the route and the number of calls. There are also other important factors which will have to be considered when the department will be preparing the estimates for highway services and rural routes, such as the topography of the area, the weather conditions and the state of roads.
For instance, in winter, transportation of mails is much easier on provincial highways, where snow-ploughs pass several times a day, than on secondary roads maintained by municipalities. I want to point out that, in the spring, when the thaw is setting in, it is almost impossible to drive on many secondary roads. It is also in winter and in spring that the contractor's vehicle is most liable to be damaged.
October 8. 1968

I would suggest to the Postmaster General the establishment of a committee made up of officials of his department and independent appraisers who, at different periods during the year, would accompany the contractor to perform the field work. Such a committee would then realize that a highway service and a rural mail delivery in the Gaspe peninsula or in northern New Brunswick are entirely different from those in the Niagara Falls or Vancouver areas.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer) has just recently established a committee travelling throughout Canada, in order to learn about housing conditions.
The Postmaster General could do likewise to determine regional standards which would direct the officials of his departments to assess the highway and rural route services.
Mr. Chairman, before closing my remarks, I am asking the House to pass the resolution under consideration. Since the Postmaster General is very understanding and anxious to co-operate with the members who are much closer to the people, I know that he intends to reconsider the removal of newspapers delivery on Saturdays, as reported in Hansard, on page 735. Even this afternoon, he mentioned he was considering the problem. Therefore, I am asking him to inform us specifically on his intentions before closing the debate.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, 1 am glad to see the Postmaster General, the designated minister of communications, has returned to his seat because for a while it seemed that the only minister in the house piloting this piece of legislation was the Minister of Fisheries. I did not think this was necessarily a coincidence.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AFFECTING RATES, ADMINISTRATION, SAVINGS BANK
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I did not miss a word of what was said.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AFFECTING RATES, ADMINISTRATION, SAVINGS BANK
speechtext:
I never assumed that the Postmaster General missed a word, but the fact is that the only minister present in the house for a short while was the Minister of Fisheries, which I thought was perhaps most appropriate. In view of the bland and general way in which the Postmaster General presented his explanation of the terms of the resolution today, Canadians across the country may think that more than what the Postmaster General said is involved here and that this thing is a little fishy. Thus the post was most aptly filled by the Minister of Fisheries in the absence of the Postmaster General.
Post Office Act
Following this opening salvo I would like to echo many of the thoughts which the hon. member for Hillsborough expressed to the minister in his remarks on the resolution before us. In this era of the great society and in extending some Irish charity from this side of the house to the minister who is supposed to have some strain of Irish in him, I wish to follow the hon. member for Hillsborough in extending congratulations to the minister on his appointment and on his presence in the house. However, I must say I found that the longer the minister spoke in his introductory remarks the more difficult it became for me to be compassionate, as one is supposed to be in this type of society, for my compassion, in opposition to Parkinson's law, diminished the longer the minister spoke as he tried to sugarcoat his way with bland generalities. In bringing to the attention of the house the exotic world of communication satellites, he tried to divert our attention from some very real flaws in the resolution.
My only conclusion, after listening to the minister and trying hard to be charitable, is that the just society, which many people tried to define during the election campaign, is simply a slogan. Therefore I feel I am being charitable in the circumstances in view of this bill in saying that the just society is one in which you pay more and get less. Certainly that is just what is proposed in this bill.
In trying to resolve the problem of how much compassion I should show in extending my congratulations to the minister and having listened to him offer a bouquet to the employees of his department, I wondered at the minister's words in speaking of the turmoil of the strike last summer when he said that the strikers, in his own words, "respected the law and demonstrated their respect for the law". There was no real doubt in the minds of Canadians about whether or not the employees of the post office demonstrated their respect for the law. There is not much doubt either on the part of the public in general that it is the government which must discharge its responsibility to govern this country. I am not going to get off the track, but it was interesting to see the minister put up this straw man and then digress by talking about satellites, telephones, electronic highways and the like.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
In listening to the minister's discussion of the strike I began to wonder whether or not the proposals in this resolution and the pending bill do emanate from the strike in the

October 8. 1968
Post Office Act
sense that the government, because of the summer doldrums, was perhaps surprised that the public did not react more violently during the early days when postal service was cut off. I do not know what was contained in the interoffice memos of the Post Office Department. Certainly there was a period of ten days or perhaps even two weeks when the public did not seem to be organized in the sense that there was much vocal criticism of the lack of postal service. I wonder in my own mind whether perhaps the postal strike of last summer has not been one of the catalysts that produced this resolution and the bill to follow, since the minister seems prepared to go far beyond what his predecessor was prepared to do just last winter.
I suggest that if this is the type of reasoning that has prompted consideration of this resolution and the progressive press announcements that have been made in an attempt to precondition Canadians to these drastic changes, then the minister is going to find out that the postal service is still very important to Canadians. While we may talk about expanding telecommunications and satellites, the postal service is the glue which holds our national fabric together. I submit that these quick suggestions for such drastic changes touch the raw nerve of most Canadians. Certainly there is no question about the need for some change in rates. However, when we see rate increases on the one hand with a reduction of service on the other, then we get some understanding of the type of renovation and reform this Postmaster General would like to bring to the post office.
It would have been rather amusing, if it were not so serious, to hear the minister suggest in a glib way that we have to buy this package holus-bolus, that if we do not do so we are neanderthal; we are against progress and against change. The minister mentioned there had been no change in the rates since 1954. Some members of the press have said that now we have a majority government, that government can move boldly to make the drastic changes necessary. It is a fact that since 1954 there have been majority governments. The fact that some governments moved carefully and cautiously, long before the just society was conceived, illustrates the perplexity and complexity of some of the issues raised in this resolution.
It is a little disappointing to me that this minister, who I think has some good ideas for reform in theory, should try to glibly give us the sugar pill. I certainly hope that when we are discussing the bill the minister will tell us
[Mr. Nowlan.l
what he proposes to do because there are fundamental implications here that go far beyond the post office itself. It is an unfortunate fact which Canadians seem to have accepted, but since 1935 the Liberal party has been in power for 27 of those 33 years. If things were so drastic and horrible, it is rather surprising to me that this party which formed the government for the majority of the time since 1935 did not move with a little more dispatch, a little more imagination and innovation, to correct some of the wrongs about which the Postmaster General told us. They certainly have had a chance to innovate and to suggest changes. I think it is a little too easy to suggest, after constructive criticism from outside the house, that we are all against change.
So far as rates and service are concerned, the hon. member for Hillsborough asked many legitimate questions. I want to concentrate a little on the rates and some of the implications contained in these rate changes. Before doing that I should like to digress for a moment and congratulate the minister sincerely on the letter that we received today, giving his second and sober thoughts concerning the rural mail contract dilemma. The letter dated October 7, which I presume was directed to all members of parliament, indicated that the rural mail contracts will be considered and assessed on a just basis. In effect, these contractors will be paid for some of the equipment they did not use. This certainly is a constructive attitude on the part of the minister and goes much further than his statement on October 1 when he said that he had sober thoughts and second thoughts but the second thoughts were the same as the first. Now, his sober thoughts and second thoughts recognize the legitimate case of the rural mail contractors in Canada. I did want to congratulate the minister upon that, without any backhanded compliment being intended.
The other change upon which I hope the minister will report when we are considering the new bill is the recommendations of the Glassco commission for improving the postal service. How many of these recommendations have been implemented since 1962 to update the postal service? If some of them have not been implemented, perhaps the minister could give the reasons why certain recommendations in this very constructive report have not been followed.
With these two digressions on the rural mail contractors and this question of change,
October 8. 1968

which is not a pill we can accept on this side of the house, I should like to comment on part of the minister's remarks. He mentioned that one of the reasons for the rate change was to ensure that newspapers and periodicals bore their fair share of the cost. I believe the hon. member for Surrey asked about international agreements, and certainly the one with the United States. I wonder how the minister reconciles these suggested changes to increase rates with the Canadian users of second and third class mail? There is a case for rate change, but how can he reconcile the statement he made that newspapers and periodicals shall bear their fair share of the cost when he knows, and I know, that the problem in connection with the newspaper and periodical business is the great influx of printed matter from the United States. This printed material contributes no revenue to our coffers because, under the international agreement, it comes into Canada basically on a postage free basis.
I believe that the suggestion that the increase in second and third class postal rates is going to solve the problems of the post office detracts from the real problem, the influx of printed material from the United States which, as a result of the international agreement, is carried by our post office on an almost postage free basis. The fact that we are now going to increase second and third class mail rates on this side of the border cannot help but aggravate the extremely involved law of copyright in connection with printing and publishing inasmuch as United States printing and publishing firms now have such a tremendous advantage over Canadian printing and publishing firms because of the vast numbers of such firms in the United States.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
As I understand the minister's remarks, by increasing the second and third class rates we will not only have a natural imbalance as a result of the volume of printed and published matter but there will be even more incentive to printing and publishing companies in the United States to send their material to Canada, thus making Canadian printing and publishing that much less competitive. This second and third class mail is dropped into United States post office boxes at United States rates; it crosses the border into Canada and in effect is carried postage free under the international agreement. I think the question asked by the hon. member for Surrey is most relevant in trying to shed some light on the
Post Office Act
problem of second and third class mail without everybody being whipped up into an emotional state about how the poor postman in Canada is carrying a lot of mail too cheaply at subsidized rates. That is why I subscribe wholeheartedly to the remarks made by the hon. member for Hillsborough. I think that once we get through the resolution stage this matter should be referred to a committee, where those directly and indirectly involved could present briefs and make submissions. This would not only help educate hon. members but also inform the public about the far-reaching implications of these proposed changes.
Another point about Canadian and United States publishing and printing is that publications of this sort are assessed for federal sales tax of 12 per cent or for provincial sales tax of 5 to 8 per cent. The minister talks of the post office paying its own way and I am wondering whether that factor has been considered. Publications of other media such as radio and television pay no such sales tax.
Another very large employer and earner of dollars for this country is the paper industry. Since the wage increases were awarded last august, out of the blue has come the press statement of the minister that these rate, increases, which range between 66 and 100 per cent, will come into effect. This statement was made without any real consultation with the industry or opportunity given to the industry to submit briefs dealing with possible discrimination against the publishing industry as a result of these rate charges that the television and radio media do not pay.
As we already know, Mr. Chairman, the C.B.C. is heavily subsidized by tax dollars. In view of the fact that there is this discrimination to which I referred and that these increases range from 66 to 100 per cent, which amounts in total to an increase of from 17 to 20 per cent depending upon province, the plea of the minister to make the post office operation a pay as you go proposition would seem to fall on deaf ears unless some explanation is given of why the publishing and printing industry has been, under the proposals of the minister, singled out to pay its own way.

Perhaps the minister has some facts and figures as to exactly how much is involved in regard to these publications that do not pay sales tax.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AFFECTING RATES, ADMINISTRATION, SAVINGS BANK
speechtext: The government would not have any figures of that kind.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour will have his chance to take the floor. This is not the house of another province and he has to govern himself by the rules of this house. It may be difficult for him but he will have to restrain himself.
As I say, some of these communications publications pay no sales tax and do not pay the higher rates. The transmission facilities of the C.B.C. radio and television services are publicly owned; yet they are still subsidized by the government.
In these areas alone, there are legitimate questions that I think the minister has to answer before this matter can proceed much further. For example, there is the question of the five day delivery week. The hon. member for Hillsborough and others will be striking out more forcefully on this subject and also on the question of rural mail contracts and deliveries. If the minister progresses as fast with the development of communication satellites as he is progressing with these drastic changes that he wants to make, then

we may be faced with the ludicrous situation of some satellite going to the moon and back before some of the people in rural areas of this country read about it. That is what will happen unless something is quickly done about the newspaper situation.
The question of a five day week is not simply a matter of giving our postal workers a two day week end, because they have it now. I think that the public is being a little misguided if it thinks that this legislation breaks new ground by giving our postal workers a five day week.

I thank hon. members for their indulgence. There is another way in which the rural mail contractor can be affected. Perhaps the minister is aware of it so I will not belabour it; other hon. members may raise it.
We must also consider when talking of a five day week how businesses in our cities will be affected. The minister has stated that the mails will still move. If a letter is dropped into a post box in Vancouver on Friday night, will it still arrive in Toronto on Monday morning? There may be an easy answer to that.
Another problem that might not be so easy to answer concerns freight forwarders. These freight forwarders do business by bills of lading which they have to pick up at their customer's box before they can process the freight. This, Mr. Chairman, together with the five day week and the delivery in Toronto on Monday of a letter posted in Vancouver on Friday, are matters of legitimate concern not only to those in our cities but also to those in rural areas where mail is carried on Saturdays.
I am not going to say anything further because I know that other hon. members have a lot more to say about these drastic changes in what, to me, is a most vital service that affects more Canadians than any other.
October 8, 1968

[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)

subtopic: AMENDMENTS AFFECTING RATES, ADMINISTRATION, SAVINGS BANK
speechtext:
I will not be too long, Mr. Chairman. In this instance I support the minister. Sometimes, I confess, it takes me longer to support a minister than to oppose him.
To come to the point, it seems that hon. members opposite are discussing the liquidation of our postal service. From what I understand of this resolution it does not mean the end of our postal service. Mr. Chairman, I started my remarks with congratulations for the honourable minister. Allow me here to show him my sympathy because, after all, having been in the minister's seat for barely two months, he is already forced to extend a begging hand.
We very well realize that he is facing increased operating costs. He is at the head of a Department with employees scattered in all parts of Canada. His employees must pay their taxes as "all workers do. All sorts of taxes have been added to the costs of the various services which the department must use.
The minister must cope with pay increases claimed by his staff who these past years have had to wrestle with increases in federal, provincial, municipal and school taxes. All increases in taxes, both direct and indirect, have pushed upwards the costs of the services required for the good operation of that department.
Of course, the operator of a fleet of trucks for instance, will have to consider the higher operating costs of his vehicles because of direct or indirect taxes. The costs of materials

The minister must face up to the high cost of labour. He has to cope with the high rents for buildings not owned by his department.
The minister is also at grips with the rise in construction costs and the department lets contracts to other departments for the construction of the buildings it requires.

Increases in revenues brought about through efficiencies, rate adjustments and larger volumes were offset constantly by the cost of increased services, additional personnel, rising labour costs and higher transportation charges.

I should like to conclude by summarizing my argument. First of all, the Post Office Department is not like the Department of National Health and Welfare; it is not like the government's area development program; it is not in the category of national medical care. It is a service for which people expect to pay. People who receive good postal service expect to pay for good service.
When second class mail is subsidized to the extent of 78 per cent by the taxpayers of this country and the people of Canada recover only 22 per cent-and many of these people are the "little people" for whom members are concerned-when the Post Office has a deficit approaching $100 million, when reforms must be initiated in first and second class rates to pave the way for needed changes in third class mail rates, then I say the evidence is overwhelming for the need for reform in this area. We have to bring postal rates and service into the twentieth century. If the opposition members want to serve the Canadian
