speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Chairman, I want to congratulate the Postmaster General on his appointment. After congratulating him, I should like to remind him that he is sitting in the seat that has a very high mortality rate. It carries a death rate of one per year over the last eight years. I do not know if he is fully aware of the great risk he is taking, particularly when he introduces this particular bill. I was very interested in listening to the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour. I was unable to decide whether he was preaching for a call or wanted to convince himself of the correctness of the attitude he was taking.
I should like also to congratulate the minister upon taking another look at the plight of the rural mail carrier. He seems to have listened not only to the members of the opposition but to members on his own side and looked at the unfairness of the decision he originally took. I want to congratulate him because I think a man is bigger when he can take a look at some of these things and then decide what is fair and right. I believe the minister has gone quite far in correcting the situation, but he still has not allowed these rural mail carriers full compensation. Their gas and oil and a few other things may be deducted. I hope he does not put these deductions on a mileage basis and charge the rural mail contractors seven cents a mile for the miles they did not travel.
I have a great deal of respect for people who work inside and outside of post offices. They have a rigid system to which to adhere, and some of them are even spied upon as they work. Those who work outside have to face elements of weather and risk, the cold and the wet, as well as the rush and hurry of people who overload them at certain periods of the year. Having said this, I must say I do not believe there was any necessity for a strike in July. I feel that this parliament must accept some of the responsibility for the str.ke. Over the years since 1956 the reforms needed in the Post Office Department were pointed out over and over again. In other words, Mr. Chairman, the postal employees were forced into a position of having to strike. This government, and to some extent previous governments, must accept the blame for this situation.
I do not believe it is proper to give employees in an essential service such as the postal service the right to strike. I believe the very nature of their service denies the 29180-61
Post Office Act
right to strike. My reason for saying this is best explained by an incident that took place in the city of New York when I was visiting there this summer. A medical doctor, a surgeon, happened to tell me that since we had a postal strike in Canada, that he had sent a pathological report to a patient of his in the city of Montreal, but the report had been turned back at the border because there was no mail delivery. This was a critical case, and I suppose the same thing could happen all along the border from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Cancer cells had been picked up in the specimen they had examined from this patient, so it was very important that the patient receive the report. We thought about what to do, and I said, "Why don't you send him a telegram and ask him to call you?" This is what the doctor did, because these reports are confidential. I am mentioning this case because there were many other such cases perhaps in which reports were not received until the strike was over. This is not a laughing matter, and could be a matter of life and death.
The strike also affected pensioners and those on welfare. These people run close to the line and when they do not receive their cheque hardship is often caused and suffered. Then, too, we must consider the loss of business and the lost orders. There were millions of dollars lost during this strike. Therefore I say that the responsibility for the strike rests squarely on the shoulders of the Postmaster General and the government. He cannot get out of it. If these employees had been treated fairly and honestly, I do not believe there would have been any strike. I think it is up to us, up to parliament, to make sure that these employees receive a fair, honest deal so that there is no reason for a strike. Surely, in this day and age there are ways for employees and employers to get together with a neutral arbitrator to come to a just decision. As a matter of fact, I would blame the government for this strike because they did not correct the faults that were pointed out in the past.
The minister referred to rising costs as a reason for increasing postage rates. I want to ask him if the efficiency of his Post Office, with all the computers and technological advances we have today, should not have been able to keep up with these rising costs? This is no excuse whatever. If business firms operating across Canada do not keep up with rising costs, then they are out of business. No one knows that better than the Postmaster

October 8, 1968
Post Office Act
General because he is a graduate in economics. The minister said that 80 per cent of the postal business is done during five days of the week. If the service is reduced, it will mean that one in five will be hurt, and this is a fairly large segment of our community. One result will be that mail that goes out on Friday will not be delivered until the following Monday, especially in rural areas.
Now, we propose to go backwards in this Post Office Department. We propose to put up costs by $8.5 million in increased postage alone, first class. I think the Postmaster General and also the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour realize quite well that by increasing costs, about which we have been preaching in parliament both before and since the hon. member came here, you cause inflation. The Postmaster General is adding to this inflation. He argues where in the world will we get the money to pay for this hundred million deficit if we do not increase charges to individuals or firms using the postal facilities? Mr. Chairman, this is inflationary.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
The cost of money orders has also increased. Apparently they are not competitive any more it is easier and cheaper to write a cheque. It looks as though the Post Office is not efficient enough to make them pay. The Postmaster General is a brilliant man in the field of economics, and I am wondering why he has to take this step backward instead of trying to make this department efficient enough to overcome the problem.
I have been receiving some mail that objects to this step that he is taking, Mr. Chairman. I have also read a lot of press articles that criticize it. The Postmaster General admitted today that he either had a hot press or a cool press, depending on what he read. I should like to read an article that I received in the mail yesterday headed: "More 'Go!', Less 'No', is what Post Office needs". The article goes on:
The announcement by Postmaster General Klerans of the cutting off of any Saturday mail services, effective February 1, is merely the latest in a series of retrogressive measures by which the Post Office has steadily diminished the standard of its services.
I am sure that the Postmaster General knows much better than I do that years ago penny postage was inaugurated. Before that time sending a letter cost $1 more or less. Generally the person who received it paid the dollar. The sender did not. Poverty in those

days dictated that if a letter was in a certain handwriting you did not pay the dollar, but returned it to the Post Office. It then went back to the dead letter office and finally I suppose, to the sender. That was some way to run the Post Office. Then the penny postage was tried and the Postmaster General knows what happened. Mail increased tremendously, until today the British post office system is one of the finest in the world and, as the Postmaster General knows, is paying its way.
This article to which I refer, Mr. Chairman, is interesting because it goes on to say:
In no other field have Canadians experienced so drastic a reduction in service, accompanied by so marked an increase in cost;-
The Postmaster General has not been here too long, but he is making his mark. But what a mark!
-in no other field do Canadians pay so much more for so much less.
It is typical of the defeatist approach of Canada's post office authorities that they should approach this latest problem of financing from the negative side. Faced with any policy decision, Canada's postal chiefs invariably resolve them by simply eliminating or reducing services, instead of improving and modernizing them and developing new sources of revenue. The result has been to give Canadians, in this age of expansion and acceleration, a standard of mail service that is slower, less frequent and less convenient than that enjoyed by previous generations in what we regard as a more leisurely age.
As a recent round-the-world survey showed, people in rural England enjoy a better standard of service than the best that can be found in supposedly sophisticated Toronto, while residents in many of the world's capitals enjoy a range and speed and frequency of mail service beyond a Canadian's wildest dreams.
The difference in approach of Canada's Post Office and that of more advanced countries can be seen in the advertisements in British newspapers. The British post office buys ads to encourage the British public to make better use of mail facilities, stressing the cheapness of such service and the speed and convenience of the medium, increasing revenue by increasing volume.
How are the government going to do this in view of the present path that they are following?
By contrast Canada's Post Office buys ads only to warn Canadians of reductions in service, to sector them about deadlines (No Christmas mail will be delivered if posted after such-and-such a date!) or to warn about some new category of mail which will not be accepted. For all of this, Canadians pay an exorbitant rate which has increased in proportion as the standard of service has declined. Presumably, such a policy can only reflect an official post office view that the ideal aimed at is one of no mail at all, at enormous public expense.
It is time that all this was changed. It is time that the Post Office was brought into the 20th century.
October 8. 1968

That is what I had hoped this new Postmaster General would do.
It is time that new procedures were introduced, utilizing new computer-era technology, to both reduce costs and speed up service. It is time the Post Office campaigned aggressively for new standards of revenue, new standards of service. The only way this can be achieved is to introduce, from the world of business, a whole new administrative executive-[DOT]
We have introduced a man of business, and I am hoping that he will see the light.
-to replace the men who presently head our post office system. Only by removing these fuddie-duddies, with their archaic, pigeon-hole concepts and negative outlook, can our postal services be streamlined to a standard worthy of this great and growing country.
I am sure that the Postmaster General would like to see some more of these editorials because they are very interesting.
In concluding, Mr. Chairman, may I say that cutting off the rural mail carriers' Saturday deliveries increases the cost of doing business, and rightly this must be considered. A rural mail carrier is all set to go, but is now going to be deprived of one day of service. He requires a motor vehicle and needs to keep it operative for six days a week, but now he will only use it on five days.
The Postmaster General referred to the possibility of amalgamating rural routes. I do not know which routes the minister was thinking of, but some that I am familiar with have as many as 300 to 400 patrons. Two such routes would mean delivering at the rate of 60 to 80 patrons an hour for a 10 hour day. I am not saying that this is the general rule, but some routes do have that number of customers, particularly tourist areas in the summer. If the Postmaster General is unaware of this I would be only too pleased to furnish him with the information.
Let us suppose that some routes are amalgamated and service is cut down. Mail will go out from ten to twelve o'clock in the morning and will be sorted by twelve o'clock. By the time the carrier gets around his route he will be ready for his bedtime meal, Mr. Chairman. If the Post Office is unable by new methods of procedure to keep costs down, then I think we will have to take another look at this sacred cow. We give $150 million to the C.B.C. without quibble. We also give money to transport and other departments. We pump millions of dollars into them.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The Postmaster General is trying to balance his accounts before he has had a chance 29180-611
Post Office Act
to look into the problems of the department. I would expect a man of his brilliance and background to introduce new methods of cutting costs. After all, Mr. Chairman, our old age pensioners cannot afford colour television or the luxury of flying, but they do like to write letters to friends. Not long ago I saw four old people in a home who had been writing letters for two hours or more. One of their joys was to send mail out to their friends and hear from them.
I am sure the minister has not studied this problem enough, or with sufficient care. I hope that after the resolution stage the minister will look at the matter with great care and apply the solutions to it that he should be capable of formulating.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I join with other hon. members who have taken part in this debate in welcoming the Postmaster General to this house. He may think we have strange ways of expressing the warmth of our welcome; really, we are trying to make him an instant member of the club, by opposing his first measure.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.

speechtext:
As
the minister knows, I have already indicated that we feel he is giving us a rather large package, some elements of which we are allowed to vote on but some elements of which we are not. In our view the package adds up to increased charges and decreased service, and therefore we do not like it and, as it stands now, we intend to vote against it.
I believe there is merit in the suggestion made by the hon. member for Hillsborough that this matter be referred to a standing committee of the house. If there are sound social and economic arguments in favour of this measure, which I doubt, I think it might be a good idea t o give officials who can expound these arguments a chance to do so before the members of a standing committee. I am convinced that if the minister were to indicate that this would be done, debate on second reading would be quite short. We would not want to spin out that debate if we had the opportunity of having this matter considered in a standing committee of this house.
The arguments for the changes the Postmaster General is proposing-changes on the one hand involving increased charges and, on the other hand, involving decreased service- are based on two companion cliches. We have

October 8, 1968
Post Office Act
heard both of them several times tonight. The first is that the post office service must be put on a pay its own way basis. The second is that there is a $100 million deficit which must be taken care of and, of course, the only way to take care of it is by increasing the charges for postal services.
May I take a moment on the first of these two companion cliches, even though colleagues who have preceded me have touched on it, as still others no doubt will. Despite what the hon. member for Bumaby-Seymour suggested a while ago, the post office service is not unlike other services provided by government. Many services provided by government at all levels do not, in themselves, pay their own way. That is, they do not directly gather in revenue equal to their cost. But the services are good for the community as a whole, good for society, good for the country, and therefore, in the long run, they are profitable to us even though in the actual bookkeeping they seem to run at a loss.
So far as government is concerned education does not pay its own way; indeed, it is all pay and no income. But surely, education pays tremendously in the life of the country. National defence does not pay its own way, but it is there if we need it. So one could go on talking of many services. I suggest if one tries to imagine a country without a postal service, without communications, he would realize how impoverished our life would then be. In other words, the value of having a postal service is immeasurably greater than the disadvantage from any deficit that may result from the rate structures we have at the present. I think, therefore, that the Postmaster General should not expect us to swallow his legislation just because he and some of his supporters keep talking about the necessity of the postal service to pay its own way.
The second of the two companion cliches was expounded very loudly a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour. He said, "There it is; we have a $100 million deficit. It must be recouped. What other way is there to do that except by raising the postage rates?" He chided the opposition for opposing this way of recouping losses, as though we liked the deficit or wanted the country to go into the red.
There are many other areas of government service where there is a deficit and where revenue has to be raised. But because those other areas are service areas we recognize that there is a case for collecting the deficit not just from the direct users of the service
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) .1
but from the taxpayers as a whole. I have searched my memory to recall what the Postmaster General said about the Carter report. It seems to me that at some point along the way he expressed interest in it and said it was a useful document. In any event, I commend it to him in support of the proposition that there are services that are best paid for, not by direct charges to the specific users of those services, but by a levy imposed according to ability to pay because of the benefit that everyone obtains from that service as a whole.
The Postmaster General and others said that some of us on this side of the house were defending business because we did not want business to pay more for its first class mail. I submit we are not defending business at all. If there is a $100 million deficit, we want that made good through steeper taxation by implementing the Carter report. We think that this is a fairer way to take care of this deficit than by exacting a charge of 1 or 2 cents extra on every first class letter that is written by everybody in this country, be that person a businessman, housewife, old age pensioner, or what have you. This is just plain, ordinary regressive taxation.
I suggest, therefore, after all the vaudeville we heard and watched half an hour ago is over, the plain fact of the matter is that the arguments for the Post Office paying its way and for meeting this deficit by charging an extra one or two cents on first class postage fall to the ground. But I accept the proposition of the hon. member for Hillsborough that this matter be referred to the standing committee so that it can be studied and, so to speak, got at a little more rationally than has been the case today in this committee of the whole.
I wish to raise three more points on which I shall not take undue time. First, we think it is unnecessary and unfair to raise the first class postage rate to six cents. We think this is a hardship-not on business people; many of them can well afford it-it is a hardship or will be a hardship on many people, even though the number of letters they may write in a month or year may be few.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
We also think it is inconsistent for the government to talk about putting the service on a pay-its-own-way basis and then to say that a letter which goes across the street or a letter which goes into a rural post office and is shifted to a box only a few feet away, should pay the same rate as a letter sent from Vancouver to St. Johns. If the principle is argued
October 8, 1968

at one point, why is it dropped at another? We think the whole concept of the six cent rate, and the concept of all first class mail paying the same rate, are false, and therefore we shall vote against this resolution.
There is another area in which we suspect we are being sold a bill of goods. I have in mind the fact that the minister has not yet given us precise details as to what will happen to the rates for second and third class mail. We have made the point many times that in our view the so-called junk mail should pay its way. We think the big newspapers, the catalogues from the department stores and so on should pay their way. The minister should not be asking writers of first class letters to pay more so as to make up for deficits brought about by the carriage of these other classes of mail at a loss.
At the same time we think there is an essential unfairness about the attitude taken by the minister inasmuch as he makes no distinction among the various categories of second and third class mail. Consideration should be given, for example, to the position of charitable organizations, groups such as the War Amputees Society, which has no doubt written to other hon. members as it has to me, and similar organizations which send out mail at less than the first class rate. In my opinion it is unfair that they should be grouped with those who send out newspapers, catalogues and junk mail.
There are organizations of various kinds which do have special claims. I think the same might be said about Christmas cards. After all, the sending of Christmas cards is a tradition in our society, and the inclusion of Christmas cards among some of the other categories which are to be charged higher rates represents a failure to distinguish among the various classes of mail.
As the Post Office Act is drawn up, we have an opportunity to vote only on the proposals which affect the first class rate; we do not have the opportunity to vote on the other rates which are covered in the general provisions of the act. The minister told us the other day when he made one of his announcements that he intended to make these declarations from time to time, so that when we got to the legislation we would have the complete picture before us. Yet today, when one of my colleagues was speaking, the hon. gentleman suggested he was talking about matters not relevant to the resolution. This demonstrates that there are some provisions,
Post Office Act
some rates, over which he has complete control. He can laugh at us here in the House of Commons. There are only two or three things for which he has to come to parliament to get approval-the first class rate, for instance. This is a strong argument in favour of the proposal made by the hon. member for Hillsborough that the whole measure might well go before a standing committee for thorough examination, with the officials of the department present to answer questions and to let us know the theory which forms bases for these decisions.
I wish to comment also on the proposal to reduce the postal service to five days a week. The hon. member for York East tried to suggest that this was only for a trial period, and that if it did not work the six day service could be restored. Well, we have heard that before. The Postmaster General did not say that. He knows that if the Saturday service is dropped it will probably be gone for a long time if not for good. We recognize the desire for a five day week, as far as the employees are concerned. Post Office employees generally do work a five day week, and the hope is that some day they will work a four day week or, if that is not possible, a seven or eight month year. These are the kinds of changes we stand for and the kinds of changes which will come.
I submit, however, that there are many inconveniences which will arise from the fact that letters posted on Friday will not reach their destination until Monday. I would remind the Postmaster General of the several occasions each year on which there is a holiday on the Monday. This will mean that letters posted on Thursday night or Friday will not arrive until Tuesday. We are asking for a lot of trouble by imposing this proposed five day week service.
Here is another example of something which I think is wrong in the Post Office Act. The minister has to come before parliament to get the first class rate increased by 50 per cent in the case of local delivery, or by 25 per cent in the case of out-of-town deliveries. But he does not need to come to us in connection with this even more drastic proposal to reduce delivery service to five days a week. He may be glad of that, in view of the trouble he is having in getting this postage rate increased through parliament. But surely, as the democrat I assume he is, he must find it strange to be in a position where all he has to do about the five day week is to announce it.

October 8. 1968
Post Office Act
Parliament can complain through the spokesmen of the opposition parties, but he is sitting there as boss and can put it into effect. Surely he does not agree with this practice.
I might also point out that the dropping of the delivery service on Saturday will place many people in the position of having to pay extra in order to get important communications through. The minister has told us that a special delivery service will be available on Saturdays and Sundays. Is it not likely that many people will need to have recourse to this more expensive way of having communications delivered? All in all we consider that this reduction of service to a five day basis is a retrograde step and that the minister should not proceed in it.
As I say, I have not tried to join in the show we witnessed a while ago. I think this is a very serious matter. As we see the whole package, it is one of increased charges and reduced services. We do not like that package and we have no option but to vote against the parts of it which are before us, in protest against the whole proposition. I hope the minister will indicate his willingness to accept the suggestion that after second reading, if it cannot be done earlier, the bill be sent to a committee so that it may be fully studied. Meantime, we shall vote against this regressive resolution.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, I do not agree, of course, that it is advisable to increase postal rates, as proposed now by the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans). It should be considered that this service is one of the most popular in the country now, in the sense that all the people have at least the possibility to use it, at a price which is really reasonable.
Taking into account the policy of the government which, in the last few weeks, has tended to cut down, to impose restrictions here and there, it might have been expected that following the reduction in some services, the Post Office Department would even have offered all the people of the country a rate reduction instead of an increase of one cent. But it seems that the government does not intend to do that.
It might be necessary to find another solution besides increasing that rate and I think that it might be in order to look for the real reasons for the department's deficit. It might be explained by the fact that the costs of various other departments are borne by the
[Mr. Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) .1
Post Office Department, as mentioned in that department's annual report for 1968. Would it not be in order to make a more detailed study to find out whether expenditures were excessive, whether there is an anomaly, in short whether the Post Office Department is not used as a milch-cow by other departments because, according to the volume of mail, the number of businesses and homes served and the possibilities of the post office, it seems to me that this deficit is hard to understand. I even feel that it would be one of the rare services which could show some profit.
We are not paying for poor management or, I should say, we are not asking the citizens of the country to pay for poor management. Instead we should find out exactly why there is a deficit. It seems to me that the explanations given in the annual report are not clear enough. We should be told how much is spent for premises, accounting services, issuance of cheques, employer's contributions to the pension fund and the Canada pension plan. It seems to me that we should be told exactly how all that money has been absorbed by the Post Office Department and why, in fact we have a deficit. I say that, Mr. Chairman, because, from the start, we were told that is the explanation for the deficit, since for some years now, the department was rather in a surplus position.
Therefore, we should preserve the quite popular aspect of the Post Office Department, namely that every citizen should have the opportunity to use the postal service at minimum costs. If we establish a precedent through a continuous increase in the cost of this service, it will end up unfortunately like many others as an expensive service. While every citizen now has the opportunity to use a rather low-cost service it seems that it is a bad time, in a period of restraint as we witness now, to increase this rate.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that the minister will reconsider this matter and that, in due time, he will be in a position to give up that increase.

Here is the whole matter in a nutshell. We have a postal service the operation of which shows a deficit, and we have to decide who is

going to make good the deficit. We must decide whether it will be the general public, through increased taxes, or the patrons. On that matter, I heard all sorts of remarks. I even heard the member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard), who is usually responsible, say that some persons who would like to write to cousins or nephews were abstaining from doing so because it would cost a little more every week. Is it possible to suppose that these people will spend 50 cents more if they write one letter a week, for instance. There are not many families doing that.
I heard earlier the member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) say that this is a people's service of which our people should not be deprived. It is obvious that it is popular, Mr. Chairman. If the government could give everything free of charge, it would gladly do so, but there is a principle to maintain: Someone must make good deficits. We get nothing for nothing in this world. Who is going to pay? Will it be the public at large, people who do not write letters, or those who send mail described earlier as dead-letter mail, which nobody wants, or the patrons of this service?
It seems to me that the answer is simple. Those who make use of a service must pay for it.
Someone tried to make a comparison between the C.B.C. and the Canadian National. The comparison does not stand. If the government wanted the C.B.C. to be a business concern, it would be a paying proposition, but for the government, the C.B.C. is something else. This service cannot be appraised in terms of the revenues which it can yield. Then, the C.B.C. would welcome any publicity like certain other television stations. In the case of transportation services, the same applies. They were established at a time where it was impossible to make ends meet under the circumstances. Canada was being developed, and by opening means of communication, the government was doing its duty. It is not at all the same problem. The postal service should pay its own way; we have incurred a deficit of several million dollars and we must admire the courage of the minister who has just stated: Those are the facts, those are the figures. There is no quibbling here. The deficit amounts to some million dollars. Someone must pay. Who will it be? Will the people pay through increased taxes? There, I see the opposition objecting. Will the users alone pay the costs? If taxes are increased, the opposition which is already blaming the government for having spent
Post Office Act
$400 million beyond estimates will be heard. In fact I see, it immediately pointing a finger at the government and saying: Increasing taxes is outrageous.
Mr. Chairman, let us be logical, let us be reasonable, let us be real businessmen, let us be realistic, let us be logical. If it costs so much, we shall obviously have to pay so much; someone must foot the bill. If we increase taxes, who is going to foot the bill? The poor, on whom we are showering our pity. Mr. Chairman, my impression is that without realizing it-but perhaps we even realize it

we are politicking so much that we are falling a prey to demagogy. To me, it is clear that two and two make four. It has been suggested that the matter should be referred to a committee. This reminds me of a certain maxim I am sure my English-speaking friends understand even better than I do: Too many cooks spoil the broth. The more there are people to settle a problem, the less things work out.
Let us then allow the minister to assume his responsibilities and if, one, two or three years, from now he is found to have been wrong, the voters will always have the privilege of asking him or the government to give an account of themselves. However, for the time being, they are trying to gain time by using incredible arguments.
I heard earlier one of my hon. friends on the other side of the house criticize Mayor Drapeau for having set up his lottery and taken advantage of a certain latitude granted under the Post Office Act. On the contrary, we should congratulate Mayor Drapeau for having shown such initiative, and I think that everybody-setting aside partisan feelings- would wish to have a mayor as dynamic and intelligent as Mayor Drapeau of Montreal, when it comes to municipal problems.
Mr. Chairman, I think-and I repeat once more-that the users should pay for the cost of postal services. I know that none of us like to pay, whether we can afford it or not. In fact, we do not like to pay our taxes, we do not like to pay our rent, we do not like to pay our bills at the end of the month. It hurts of course, but somebody has to pay. Would not the rational way of paying the bill be to divide it between those who use the postoffice services? It seems so obvious to me that I am surprised we had to speak for such a long time to settle the matter.
The hon. minister said: We will have to try

note he did not say it was definite-to apply restrictions on the postal service.

October 8. 1968
Post Office Act
We should wait, in all objectivity, to have proof that those restrictions are truly prejudicial to the users. It struck me how the minister stated the case, because he left us an open door when he said: It is an experiment, the matter will remain open. He did not use those terms, perhaps but that is what I understood. It will remain open and if it is proven that this is truly prejudicial to the community, we are ready to accept suggestions and reconsider our decisions. He has already done so in the field of the highway service.
Mr. Chairman, what is the meaning of that? I feel that we are still resorting to demagogy and moreover an easy demagogy. It is always easy to take the floor and say that the people are oppressed and that they have to pay beyond their means, when we all know that we are going through a difficult financial period. That does not apply only in Canada. It is an international concern. It is easy to take advantage of that situation and say that the government is unfair, that it oppresses and persecutes the poor people. Imagine: It is asking one cent more per letter, when the average Canadian does not mail a letter a week. What will that cost in a year?
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Advertising agencies, business concerns, make use of the postal service, and they are in business. They can pay for the services which brings them profits; it is not up to those who write only five, ten or at the most 50 letters a year, to pay for the others.
Mr. Chairman, to my mind the situation is so clear that we should not complicate matters with partisan or demagogic considerations. To sum up the situation, postal services cost so much they must pay their own way. The same can probably not be said about all federal government services, true enough. But, with regard to postal services, it is so true that it should be profitable, that I am of those who agree that it should be entrusted to private enterprise which would then have to take the necessary means to make ends meet. I am not saying that the solution is ideal at the present time, but I feel that, in due course, there may be good reason to study that suggestion.
And so, not only should the Postmaster General not be blamed for this bill, but we should, on the contrary, underline the courage he has proved; for, in politics, it is never profitable, at least it does not seem to be, to tell the electors: You have to pay more for the services you are provided with.

However, Mr. Chairman, I think that today the Canadian citizen is rather well informed. He is not undully impressed with demagogic considerations which used to influence him in the past. He has a craving for truth, he wants to be sure that two and two make four, he wants to know whether he is told stories or the truth even if the truth is hard to take.
I think that the Postmaster General has shown courage in introducing this legislation and other related measures which, in the long run, will prove this very simple fact, namely that someone has to pay for everything our citizens receive. Who is going to pay for it? There is no magic in our world and it seems to me that the simplest way to put it is to say that the patrons will pay for it. For this reason I unreservedly support this bill and I think that all fair-minded members should support it too.

Mr. Chairman, it has
been said that this institution, the House of Commons, is a full length mirror that unerringly reflects our capacities, mediocrities, motives, maturity and magnanimity. I thought while listening to the minister introducing this resolution to amend the Post Office Act that this saying certainly holds true and can be applied to the minister in this case and to much of the legislation in general with which we have dealt in the house.
The hon. member who has just resumed his seat, the one time independent, and now the Liberal member for Trois-Rivieres, said during the course of his remarks that too many cooks spoil the broth. This and the two preceding governments are a good example of this proverb. We have reached the stage where the deficit and inefficiency within the Post Office Department is so great-I am just taking one department as an example-that the saying has come true, and that too many cooks have spoiled the broth. I do not know how many postmasters general we have had during the past six years.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure you will agree that the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres has made my point for me. I started to talk about the resolution. This resolution including the newly proposed five day week, thus reducing the postal service available to the people of Canada and at the same time increasing the cost to the people, reflects a lack of capacity of the Trudeau government. It reflects their mediocrity; it shows their immaturity and lack of stature in their efforts to serve the Canadian people.
The Canadian people expected something far more efficient and dynamic than the measures we are getting. I can do no better, in order to make several other points-and I am sure other hon. members will agree with those points-than quote from the Sault Star. I do not often quote from the Sault Star, although the Sault familiar to me is a "suburb" of the place in which I was born, namely Plummer township, Rydal Bank, Algoma district, Ontario.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
The Sault Daily Star of Thursday, October 8 states this under the heading "Post office service must improve":
The national Post Office has been the centre of unfavourable attention from Canadians in recent months. Whether or not this situation continues remains to be seen. Certainly, there are avenues open for the Post Office to redeem itself. That is 29180-62
Post Office Act
if it has the foresight and initiative to explore these avenues.
The events of recent months which brought the Post Office into disfavour started with the postal workers' strike. This strike lasted for three weeks through July and August and depressed and irritated a public deprived of an essential service.
With the settlement of the strike came the news there would be a hike in postal rates to offset the post office deficit and pay for the postal workers' wage increases. The word was that the postage rate for all first class mail-local and out of town-would be six cents.
Let me remind the minister that this represents an increase of 20 per cent in that service which adds to the cost of living in this country. Let me quote further from this newspaper:
Then, the other day Postmaster General Eric Kierans announced that starting Feb. 1, 1969 there would be no postal deliveries on Saturday and post offices will be closed on that day. This action said the Postmaster General was necessitated to cut down office costs.
Let me intervene briefly at this point to ask in what way this will cut down office costs? Thousands of people who work in the postal department will receive the same take-home pay after February 1, 1969. I am sure no one in this house wants to lower this take home pay, but I submit that administrative costs will remain about the same. This article goes on to say:
All of this has done nothing to win friends and supporters of the Post Office among the Canadian public.
The article also states:
However, while there may be justification for these moves by the Post Office the public has justification too in expecting that accompanying these unpopular measures there will be a diligent and conscientious effort by the Postmaster General's department to streamline the present Post Office operation.
I will not read the entire article, but it goes on to state:
If there are going to be fewer deliveries and higher postal rates the public has the right to expect there will be increased efficiency in the postal delivery system as a compensatory measure.
The last paragraph states:
If the Canadian public is going to have to pay more for its post office services, and if it is going to have curtailed services then the public should expect and should demand, that the service which is provided be made far better than the service it presently enjoys.
I disagree with that last word "enjoys" in the article, to the effect that the Canadian public presently enjoys the service it gets. Surely we do not enjoy much of the service we now have. I receive complaints regarding

October 8, 1968
Post Office Act
the slowness of some forms of mail delivery, and particularly that service from Toronto and Montreal to Napanee. This is particularly so in respect of parcel post. It is used extensively by professional people such as doctors and dentists, as well as the hospitals. These people are still complaining about the slowness of the delivery of mail. As for the recent strike, any government which would allow a strike to continue at such a tremendous cost to the Canadian people, and then reduces mail service to a five day week does not have any knowledge of the needs of the Canadian people and apparently has no desire to improve this service.
I have before me a letter written by the Postmaster General. I am sure hon. members were pleased to receive this in explanation and in answer to those protests made by many of us on behalf of rural mail contractors. There are two explanations contained in this letter dated October, 1968. The first is:
To rural route contractors and those performing other small service contracts, doing the work themselves, and paid on the basis of an annual rate, we propose making the regular payment for the period which the service was interrupted, less the normal operating expenses which were not incurred while the service was not performed.
The second explanation refers to larger contracts and it says in part:
In these cases we propose to pay the contractor his direct out of pocket expenses where the contract is on a per annum basis.
All our rural mail contracts are on a per annum basis. The full cost of payments to all these contractors has been previously budgeted for and the government's attempt to save a little money at the expense of these rural mail contractors seems to be pretty small, in light of the strike which was partly the fault of the government, because of its apathy. I am not placing all the blame on the government but surely this strike resulted partly from the lack of government action.
In my riding we must deal with rural and urban problems. We have no door to door mail delivery. I say to the Minister: Let us forget about this retrograde step to a five day week. I say on behalf of the farmers in the constituency of Frontenac-Lennox and Addington, they must get daily delivery. It is one hundred years since confederation. This is 1968, not 1868. If ever we needed a daily delivery we need it now.
What about the farmers who depend on rural route deliveries for their various agriculture returns and cheques, and their daily newspapers. Many of them depend on [Mr. Alkenbrack.l
this service for these things. We do not have any house to house deliveries in my riding, but I have heard many protests from those who do in the neighbouring cities of Kingston and Belleville. I have heard the people say there that they used to get mail delivery twice a day, but that they are now getting it only once a day. They have stated that after the Trudeau government gets through with them they will only receive mail five days a week.
What about the differences in the services offered by various types of post offices? There will be no equity of service under the minister's new measure. In my riding for example I should like to compare the proposed services to be provided by the Napanee town post office and the service to be provided to the hamlet of Lavant.
The Napanee post office is owned and operated by the federal government, but under the minister's new measures no one will be able to obtain service there on a Saturday. We will not be able to buy a money order, obtain information or pick up a general delivery letter. The wickets will be closed. I hope the local people will be able to walk into the post offices and unlock their own boxes in order to get their mail. I hope the minister is not going to lock the entrance doors of the local post offices. Of course, since he is discontinuing the services of the post office savings banks, people who come to certain centres on Saturday will not be able to use them, either. This does not apply to the settled portions of Canada. I know that probably no one in my town uses post office savings methods any more, but there are people in remote areas of Canada who use the post office savings facilities, and the abolition of these services will be a hardship to them.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Let us get back to the other type of post offices. I wish to refer to the post office in Lavant. It is in a general store. The local residents who come into Lavant to do their shopping on Saturday will also ask for their mail and the storekeeper will certainly give it to them, as he should and can. I ask the minister, is this the just society? There will be no service in Napanee on Saturday, but plenty of service in Lavant. The latter is as it should be. I say again, this is 1968, not 1868.
At the same time as the minister is abolishing the daily mail service, I have just received a request which came in this week from the reeve and council of the townships
October 8. 1968

of Barrie and Miller, in the country of Fron-tenac, that rural route No. 2 to Cloyne, for example, which is now a route with a three day a week frequency be increased to a daily mail service. I told reeve Tom Neale that I would bring this matter up in the house. This is an important rural route serving many tourists in the summer and the settlers, lumbermen and tourist lodges in the winter. It should have a daily mail service the year round. If the minister put into effect his five day week program, the best we can get for these people will of course be the five day delivery. I ask for his assistance in this matter, and I am sure that it will be forthcoming. We can improve the service there, although if this measure goes through, we will not get daily service.
There is another matter against which I want to protest. It concerns the treatment of the rural mail contractors. They should be given every cent coming to them under their contracts and should not be docked at all for anything resulting from the late lamented postal strike. In the review of their contracts, as mentioned in the resolution, the existing tenders and contracts should run as they are for the remainder of the lives of these contracts. Any changes made will only cost the government more money, and moreover the government has no business interfering with contracts made in good faith and signed with reliable people. The point I wish to make is that even if these contracts are renegotiated for a five day week, in view of the rapid escalation of other costs similar bids will be made for five days a week as those made formerly for six days a week. At the present time I believe these contracts run for four years, and if those made four years ago had to be renegotiated the average bidder would ask for more money.
Much has been said in the house since the debate began regarding ways of saving money in the Post Office Department. I am sure the minister will try to do that. I do not blame him for his efforts along these lines and I want to compliment him in that regard. Our criticism must be constructive. There is much good in trying to find ways of saving money in that department. Let us hear more about this from the minister and from all sides of the house.
With regard to the effect of this legislation on local businessmen, may I point out that many businessmen pick up their mail on Saturday and examine it during the remainder of the week end. They do not necessarily
Post Office Act
look at the mail on Saturday because they are too busy on that day, especially those who are in the retail business. For that reason the post office should be open six days a week, as are those businesses.
Much has been heard here about the cost of second class mail. Of course costs are involved in handling and sorting second class mail. However most of it is no use anyway; it is more or less a public nuisance. Then, I am sure the newspaper publishers face the future knowing that it will cost them more to have their newspapers delivered. I believe that now they are sent free within a 40 mile radius. I am told that this does not apply to the dailies, or to any publication delivered house to house. Outside the 40 mile radius payment for newspapers is made according to weight. I was in contact with two editors of weeklies in my riding, and they told me this afternoon that the newspapers expect to pay more but also expect value for their money.
The matter of junk mail has been raised several times from all corners of the house. I believe we should reduce a lot of this superfluous junk mail. We get too much of it right here, as members of the house. I am not referring to legitimate mail which is sent to us by our constituents.

CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT-ALLEGED DELAY IN SUBMISSION OF RETURNS BY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other day when I brought a question before this house concerning the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act, it was suggested that I put the question on the order paper, and for this reason I am suggesting the subject be considered tonight. This act was passed in 1982 after a considerable amount of debate. Upon reviewing Hansard, I find a considerable amount of debate again took place on this subject in 1965 when amendments to the act were introduced. My reason for bringing this question before the house is that it is my opinion there is absolutely no use in this house passing legislation if there is no enforcement of that legislation. I suggest that unless there is a good reason for the lack of enforcement of the provisions of any act, then those provisions should be enforced.
The purpose of this act was to have corporations and unions file annual returns. The other day I requested a report under the provisions of this act in so far as corporations and unions were concerned, and I was told that
-the preparation of the data for the corporation report has been delayed but improvements are being made and it is our objective to be more timely in the near future.
The only return that I received from the corporation was for 1963, while I received a return from the unions for every year including 1966.
I should like to ask the minister responsible for answering this question this evening for an explanation of why the returns from the corporations are not available. Unless there is an adequate reason for the lack of such
[Mr. Mcllraith.j
DEBATES	October 8. 1968
returns in 1963. I should like to know whether the corporations are liable for the penalty outlined in section 6 of the act. If they are not liable, why not?
If the returns outlined in the report are not liable for return by the corporations, I should like to know whether there is any reason for the unions to file a return, as such, each year. If they do not file a return, are they responsible under section 6 of the act?
I noticed in Hansard that in September 1964 the then member for Port Arthur said it was obvious that the government was not enthusiastic about the bill as a whole, and that he assumed the legislation was going to waste away. I only ask that if it is the intention of the government to let this legislation waste away, then why do they not tell us, instead of leaving the act unfulfilled?
I would ask the minister to answer this question at this time, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it is of the utmost importance, particularly for myself, to know whether or not the act means what it says, and should be enforced in its entirety.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister without Portfolio):
maintopic: CORPORATIONS AND LABOUR UNIONS RETURNS ACT-ALLEGED DELAY IN SUBMISSION OF RETURNS BY CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad indeed to rise to answer the question of the hon. member for Moose Jaw. Let me say at the outset that it is certainly not the intention of this government to let this legislation waste away. If there has been-as there has-some difficulty in the beginnings in carrying out the spirit of the legislation in full, it is partly due to the fact that the broadest interpretation possible has been put upon it.
I should like to say to the hon. member that the returns have in fact been made on time, but that the difficulty has been in compiling, investigating and reporting upon the data concerned. The differentiation between union and corporation reports is due to the difficulty of dealing with two groups of reports. There are in fact 175 unions which are required to report under the terms of the act, whereas there are 40,000 corporations.
In addition, part of the investigation into corporation returns is in its nature difficult. As I have said, at the moment the corporations are not in default in filing returns and the 1967 returns are on hand. To show the difficulty involved, however, of these 25,000 returns have been fully processed and, I may say, are available for inspection, as are the previous returns, in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, which is the proper place at this stage. Some 12,000 further returns are in process of examination
October 8, 1968

and tabulation, and several thousand others are being investigated from the point of view of whether a proper return has been made.
The hon. member may understand that there is some difficulty about the existence or non-existence of corporations, which on the books could apparently be making a return. One of the difficulties involved is that of determining the ultimate ownership of the shares of a corporation. At the moment, Mr. Speaker, some 15,000 corporation returns are being investigated from this point of view. There is also the difficulty not only of pursuing the ownership of the shares and, in some cases, finding it in the hands of the corporation, but of pursuing the ownership of the said shares through the ownership of the corporation.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
So, this has been a long process. I am happy to say that the dominion statistician who is responsible in this regard is taking active measures to improve reporting procedures and bring them up to date. The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg) and other hon. members will be pleased to know that the report for the 1964 corporate returns is now in the printing stage. The report for 1965 should be available about the end of the year and it is hoped that the 1966 report will be available in the spring.
